reviewer: Independent reviewer B; did not write these articles
scope: All eleven A drafts and full matching Rust fixtures read; prose edits only. No local build, test, formatter or runtime workload.
style_standard: Clear, natural English accessible to a non-native reader. No claim of human authorship, invented personal experience or artificial grammar errors.

articles.verdict: accepted after narrowing title and explaining the stored transaction rule; publication hold retained

changes.rejected_passage: title: "Build a Small PostgreSQL Service in Rust with SQLx"
changes.replacement: title: "PostgreSQL from Rust: Make Related Writes Commit Together"
changes.reason: The original title promises a service implementation; the example is a database transaction without an HTTP service.

changes.rejected_passage: This is a useful first PostgreSQL example because it gives the database a real job: keep related changes together and reject invalid stored values. Rust helps represent the operation, but the database must enforce its part even when a request fails halfway through.
changes.replacement: The debit, credit and transfer record belong to one operation. Either all three stay in the database, or none of them do. A transaction handles that boundary, while constraints reject balances and amounts the service must never store.
changes.reason: Replace praise of the tutorial with the exact invariant and the jobs of transaction versus constraint.

changes.rejected_passage: ## Leave room for the service to be operated
changes.replacement: ## Check upgrades, pool waits and recovery
changes.reason: The original heading is awkward and vague; name the operational tasks actually discussed.

changes.rejected_passage: Keep the duplicate-request test when adding the HTTP handler. It should still finish with one transfer record and unchanged balances after the repeated attempt. A nicer response or a new service layer should not change those stored outcomes.
changes.replacement: When the HTTP handler is added, map a duplicate request to a deliberate response. It can return the earlier transfer or reject a conflicting reuse of the key. In either case, the repeated request must leave the balances at seventy and thirty and keep exactly one transfer record.
changes.reason: Replace a generic instruction to preserve tests with concrete endpoint behavior and its stored-state check.

pending_limits: Integer-credit demonstration; no HTTP implementation, complete idempotency protocol, authorization or money model. Final remote CI remains the coordinator’s responsibility.

articles.verdict: accepted after clarifying schema-marker ownership and missing-file startup handling; publication hold retained

changes.rejected_passage: The example here stores a title and a completion flag. It uses rusqlite 0.41.0 with a pinned bundled SQLite dependency. It is deliberately small enough to inspect after closing and reopening the connection. The important result is the stored row and the behavior around failure, rather than a collection of database features.
changes.replacement: The example stores a title and a completion flag using rusqlite 0.41.0 with a pinned bundled SQLite dependency. It commits one note, rolls back another, then reopens the same file. That gives us a specific answer to the empty-screen problem: which note did the app actually save?
changes.reason: Remove tutorial self-description and contrastive filler; connect the example directly to the missing data.

changes.rejected_passage: The version marker is just an integer the application manages. SQLite does not infer which migration it describes. Its [PRAGMA reference](https://www.sqlite.org/pragma.html#pragma_user_version) explains that separation. If someone changes the table and forgets the marker, the database cannot repair the migration history for them.
changes.replacement: The version marker is an integer the application manages. SQLite does not check whether version one really has the table expected by release one; its [PRAGMA reference](https://www.sqlite.org/pragma.html#pragma_user_version) leaves that meaning to the application. Update the schema and marker in the same migration transaction so a failed change does not leave them out of step.
changes.reason: Replace personification and vague migration warning with the concrete requirement already implemented in migrate().

changes.rejected_passage: Before shipping the notes store, check the path on a second launch, the message shown for an unsupported schema version, and a restore into a separate directory. Those are small checks a support report can name. The app can keep using a local database until sharing or operating the data calls for a different design.
changes.replacement: A later launch that cannot find the saved file should make that situation visible. Opening a new empty file can look exactly like a successful launch with lost notes. Keep first-run setup distinct from opening an existing store, and show the resolved location in support diagnostics. A schema-version refusal should be equally clear: the app found the file but cannot safely write its format.
changes.reason: Replace the generic pre-shipping checklist and vague technology conclusion with a specific startup failure the reader can address.

pending_limits: Ordinary connection close/reopen only; not power-loss durability, process-restart evidence or a backup implementation.

articles.verdict: accepted for ordinary primary reads after clarifying the snapshot boundary; publication hold retained

changes.rejected_passage: Repeatable Read keeps the relevant transaction snapshot rather than taking a new one for every ordinary statement. PostgreSQL establishes that view at the first query or data-changing statement, not simply when Rust allocates a transaction variable. The [SET TRANSACTION reference](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-set-transaction.html) describes both the visibility rules and when isolation may be selected.
changes.replacement: Under Repeatable Read, ordinary queries share the view established by the transaction’s first query or data-changing statement. Calling begin in Rust does not by itself take that snapshot. The [SET TRANSACTION reference](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/sql-set-transaction.html) explains when the level can be selected.
changes.reason: Shorten abstract snapshot phrasing and keep the important begin-versus-first-query distinction.

changes.rejected_passage: ## A stable read is not permission to write stale decisions
changes.replacement: ## Protect the rule when the request also writes
changes.reason: The old heading personifies permission and hides the next practical question.

changes.rejected_passage: The tiny stock example intentionally performs ordinary reads and a separate committed update. It does not test every locking clause or demonstrate a complete reservation service. Its assertions are specific: different statement snapshots under Read Committed, one shared view under Repeatable Read, and a fresh view after the transaction ends.
changes.replacement: If a report later becomes a reservation endpoint, revisit that write rule before reusing its read transaction. The <ArticleLink slug="sql-postgresql-rust-retry-whole-transaction">whole-transaction retry example</ArticleLink> shows a competing commit between a read and a write. Its retry repeats the decision from fresh data, instead of carrying a value from the earlier attempt.
changes.reason: Replace a repeated scope disclaimer with a relevant next failure and a publication-aware contextual link.

changes.rejected_passage: For the order report, decide whether its total and detail rows must describe the same database view. Keep that decision with the two-read test so a later query split does not silently change the result users receive.
changes.replacement: The order report can show a coherent order as it existed at the start of its snapshot. A later refresh can show a newer coherent version. If that is the intended behavior, keep the total and detail reads inside that boundary; the time between the two Rust calls should not decide which version each sees.
changes.reason: Replace a stock maintenance ending with a precise user-visible promise for the report.

pending_limits: Ordinary primary-database SELECT statements; no cache, replica or complete multirow invariant guarantee.

articles.verdict: accepted after simplifying serialization and making repeated decisions explicit; publication hold retained

changes.rejected_passage: This is why a transaction retry is larger than an error-handling loop around one SQL call. It repeats the database operation's decision, including any values read to choose the write. The operation also needs a stopping rule so contention cannot keep a request alive forever.
changes.replacement: Each attempt owns the read, the calculation, the write and the commit. The loop starts that whole attempt again, with a limit on how many times it can try. Keeping those steps together makes it harder to reuse the old zero by accident.
changes.reason: Replace an abstract restatement with the exact work owned by an attempt.

changes.rejected_passage: The server may reject an attempt because its observed concurrency cannot safely be accepted under the selected isolation rules. A failure at this point is a defined outcome the application needs to handle.
changes.replacement: Here PostgreSQL cannot accept both operations as if they had run one after the other, so it rejects an attempt. The application must be prepared for that result.
changes.reason: Simplify dense English and explain serialization in familiar terms.

changes.rejected_passage: The program's counter is deliberately small. It does not establish a useful contention rate, a maximum transaction throughput, or a good production backoff interval. There is no timing result to report from the ten-millisecond pause in the loop.
changes.replacement: The ten-millisecond pause is a fixture setting. For a busy service, choose a bounded delay and consider jitter so requests that fail together do not all try again together. Backoff still cannot guarantee that an attempt will succeed.
changes.reason: Replace three repeated non-benchmark disclaimers with a practical reason for a retry delay, preserving the absence of a performance claim.

changes.rejected_passage: The useful boundary is the attempt function. It owns the reads, writes, and commit decision together. Once that boundary is clear, the retry loop can stay short, and a reviewer can see exactly what will happen again.
changes.replacement: When adapting this code, look for calculations still sitting outside attempt: a chosen row, a price or a decision based on permission data. If one depends on database state that can change, decide whether it must be repeated too. A new transaction does not refresh a value that the Rust caller keeps passing back in.
changes.reason: Replace a generic approval-style closing paragraph with a concrete review action for stale values.

pending_limits: First-attempt competing write is harness coordination. SQLSTATE40001 only; unknown commit outcomes and external effects need separate treatment.

articles.verdict: accepted after separating HOT classification from a fillfactor improvement claim; publication hold retained

changes.rejected_passage: Sometimes it can avoid that work through a heap-only tuple update, usually called HOT. The name describes an optimization in the table's row storage. It does not mean the update costs nothing, and it does not apply just because the Rust code changed one small integer.
changes.replacement: Sometimes it can avoid new index entries through a heap-only tuple update, usually called HOT. PostgreSQL normally stores a new row version for an update. HOT lets that new version share an existing route from the index, provided the required columns and page space allow it.
changes.reason: Explain the mechanism near the unfamiliar name instead of using a generic warning about cheap updates.

changes.rejected_passage: The test creates a fresh table to keep unrelated row history out of the comparison. It does not infer what a busy production page looks like from one newly inserted row.
changes.replacement: The test starts with one row on a fresh page, so there is already plenty of room. The low fillfactor makes the intended setup explicit; this example does not show that changing fillfactor caused an improvement. A useful fillfactor comparison needs enough rows to fill pages under each setting.
changes.reason: Avoid implying a one-row experiment demonstrates a fillfactor benefit; specify what a real comparison would need.

changes.rejected_passage: These are assertions for the example, not results measured on an application workload. The program prints the actual counter pairs when run through CI. It also reads the final counter and label so an optimization-looking result cannot hide a write that never happened.
changes.replacement: The assertions require those pairs for this one-row layout. The program also reads the final counter and label, checking that the intended values were stored. It prints the pairs from the actual run so the observation can be kept with the table definition.
changes.reason: Remove awkward wording and repeated non-benchmark framing while retaining expected-versus-observed scope.

changes.rejected_passage: For the first investigation, save the table definition, every index definition, the counter interval, and the operation that ran during it. That record can support a useful explanation: these writes changed only the counter and qualified for HOT; this label change did not. It is a firmer starting point than assuming that a tiny Rust assignment must produce a tiny database write.
changes.replacement: An index added for a new visits dashboard can change this write path too. Review that index alongside the counter update, then compare HOT counts and the dashboard query under the proposed schema. Keep the table layout and counter interval with the result, so the next engineer can tell which writes the counts describe.
changes.reason: Replace a generic evidence checklist and rhetorical ending with the concrete effect of adding an index to the demonstrated counter.

pending_limits: One short row, B-tree indexes and ample page space. No latency, WAL-size, vacuum or production fillfactor-benefit measurement.

articles.verdict: accepted for trusted application context; hostile SQL remains explicitly outside the protection; publication hold retained

changes.rejected_passage: The source is `experiments/sql-rust/postgres-sqlite/src/bin/pg_rls.rs`. The application pool is deliberately limited to one connection so the test can examine what a later checkout sees:
changes.replacement: The source is `experiments/sql-rust/postgres-sqlite/src/bin/pg_rls.rs`. The application pool has one connection, so a later request reuses the session whose tenant setting we just changed:
changes.reason: Explain pool checkout in plain request terms and show why the one-connection setup matters.

changes.rejected_passage: The policy handles an empty custom setting as well as an absent one. That matters when a session has previously used the setting. A helper that assumes “missing” always has one representation can make a pool-reuse check fail for the wrong reason.
changes.replacement: The policy uses NULLIF to turn an empty setting into null before casting to an integer. An absent setting is also null because current_setting is called with missing_ok enabled. Neither value matches a tenant. Without the empty-string check, an integer cast could fail instead of giving the intended no-context result.
changes.reason: Replace vague representation language with the exact expression and its failure case, matching the policy source.

changes.rejected_passage:
The fixture runs against an explicitly supplied disposable PostgreSQL database. It does not create a new production login or change permissions on application tables. Every test gets its own schema, and the application role receives access only to that example schema.

When reviewing the result, retain the effective role attributes, policy definition, and returned IDs with the CI run. Avoid recording the database URLs. The question to settle is concrete: did the separate application role see the right rows, refuse the wrong write, and forget the tenant when its transaction ended?
changes.replacement: If a legitimate request suddenly returns an empty list, check which tenant the transaction selected and which role ran the query. Missing context is meant to deny access here, but silently showing an empty workspace can hide a broken request path. Report that configuration failure to the service diagnostics while keeping other tenants’ rows out of the response.
changes.reason: Remove internal test-infrastructure padding and the canned final question; give a concrete diagnostic for a denied legitimate request.

pending_limits: Trusted application chooses tenant. Arbitrary SQL under this role can choose a custom setting; this is not hostile-SQL isolation. Separate role and positive/negative behavior are exercised; other functions/views/admin access remain out of scope.

articles.verdict: accepted as durable-row recovery with notification wake-ups; complete queue protocol excluded; publication hold retained

changes.rejected_passage: title: "Use PostgreSQL NOTIFY to Wake Rust Workers, Not to Store Their Work"
changes.replacement: title: "Recover Pending Rust Jobs After a PostgreSQL Listener Reconnects"
changes.reason: Lead with the problem solved rather than a stock contrastive title; durable scan remains the article’s distinctive topic.

changes.rejected_passage: Keeping insertion and notification together also avoids the ordinary case where a row commits but a later application call to send its wake-up fails. It still does not make the wake-up durable for a disconnected listener. The table is what closes that gap.
changes.replacement: Keeping insertion and notification together avoids committing a row and then failing in a separate call that should send its wake-up. A listener that was disconnected can still miss the event. When it returns, it finds the row through the pending-work query.
changes.reason: Use a concrete sequence instead of abstract gap-closing phrasing.

changes.rejected_passage: The example uses a new listener object to make the gap explicit. It does not simulate every network failure or claim that dropping the object reproduces a particular production outage. The useful sequence is simply that job two commits before the new subscription exists.
changes.replacement: The example creates a new listener after job two commits. That gives it no subscription during the commit, which is the particular gap being tested. It is a controlled absence, rather than a test of SQLx reconnecting after a physical network failure.
changes.reason: Shorten repeated evidence disclaimers while keeping the actual test scope precise.

changes.rejected_passage: The program marks the pending work done and verifies the scan is empty. Its assertions cover the stored rows and both notification phases, not merely a log message saying reconnect succeeded.
changes.replacement: Do not assume one event means one job. PostgreSQL can combine repeated notifications with the same channel and payload within a transaction. A producer could insert several jobs and emit one wake-up. The worker must scan the pending rows instead of processing just the number of events it received.
changes.reason: Replace self-referential verification prose with a documented delivery property that explains why the durable scan is necessary.

pending_limits: Controlled listener absence, not physical reconnection fault injection. Single consumer; no atomic multiworker claim or durable external-effect protocol.

articles.verdict: accepted as an unchanged manual-decoder compatibility demonstration; publication hold retained

changes.rejected_passage: There is also a database transaction boundary to respect. A newly added PostgreSQL enum value cannot be used in the same transaction before that addition commits. These are two separate readiness checks: when the database can use the value, and when the application fleet can handle it.
changes.replacement: When adding a label to the existing database enum used here, the migration must commit before another statement uses that label. Separately, every reader that can receive it needs a way to handle it. Finishing the migration answers only the first question.
changes.reason: Scope the commit rule to the existing enum in the fixture and simplify abstract fleet-readiness wording.

changes.rejected_passage: The fixture reads the database enum as text and passes that text to the unchanged decoder. That makes the compatibility failure explicit without depending on a particular derive macro's error wording. It is not a test of SQLx's generated enum decoder; the boundary here is the old Rust application's accepted values.
changes.replacement: The program reads the database enum as text, then calls this unchanged function. It tests the values the old application accepts. It does not exercise SQLx’s derived enum decoder; if the shipped application uses one, keep that actual decoding path in its compatibility check too.
changes.reason: Make the manual-versus-generated decoder limitation direct and give the reader a specific next check.

changes.rejected_passage: These checks are intentionally asymmetric. The database accepting the new label is expected. The old decoder rejecting it is also expected. The purpose is to expose a rollout condition the release process must address, not to pretend that a green migration automatically means all readers are compatible.
changes.replacement: Consider a worker that decodes a whole page of orders before processing any. One processing row could stop that page, including older pending orders the worker normally understands. Exercise the real batch or endpoint around the decoder, so the rollout plan accounts for how far a rejected value spreads.
changes.reason: Remove abstract description of the test and show a concrete consequence beyond one decode failure.

changes.rejected_passage: Before enabling the writer, the release record should answer three concrete questions: has the enum addition committed, which readers have been checked, and what will handle rows written before a rollback? The small fixture makes the first failure visible. The deployment plan must decide how users are protected from the second.
changes.reason: Remove the final checklist rather than restating the rollback obligation already explained in this section.

changes.rejected_passage: PostgreSQL enum changes have different costs and restrictions from editing a Rust enum declaration. Preserve the database migration history and the application compatibility checks together. The old decoder test is useful precisely because it can remain unchanged across several candidate rollout plans.
changes.reason: Remove a generic reminder and repeated defense of the retained decoder, already covered where the decoder is introduced. End on the concrete rollback requirement.

pending_limits: Retained manual decoder only, not a real previously released artifact or SQLx derive path. No rollout gate or compatibility presenter implemented.

articles.verdict: accepted after correcting write-lock acquisition wording and separating two recovery paths; publication hold retained

changes.rejected_passage: It does, but concurrent reading and writing is a different promise from concurrent writers. SQLite still serializes writes to one database. WAL changes how committed data and readers interact; it does not turn every connection into an independent writer.
changes.replacement: WAL lets a reader continue while a writer works, but writes to one database still take turns. A second connection can read committed data without being allowed to start another write. That is the distinction the two-connection example below checks.
changes.reason: Replace abstract concurrency terminology with the behavior the reader will see.

changes.rejected_passage: Immediate transactions can make a write-intended operation acquire its write position early. That can simplify failure handling: the transaction learns about contention before doing a collection of reads. It still has to handle a failed begin, and it should not acquire the write lock long before it needs it.
changes.replacement: BEGIN IMMEDIATE tries to acquire the write transaction at the start. If another writer holds it, begin can fail before the application has made decisions from a set of reads. This can simplify a read-then-write operation. It does not reserve a place in a fair queue, and the lock should be held only for the database work that needs it.
changes.reason: “Write position” can imply a guaranteed queue position. Describe lock acquisition and the failed-begin path precisely.

changes.rejected_passage: The example does not build a retry framework. It separates two concrete outcomes and demonstrates the transaction boundary each needs. That is enough to stop treating all busy errors as one instruction to sleep longer.
changes.replacement: After ordinary writer contention, a later attempt may run once the writer releases its lock. After BUSY_SNAPSHOT, the old read transaction must end before the decision can be repeated with a fresh view. Keep those two recovery paths distinct in the error handler.
changes.reason: Replace tutorial self-assessment with the two actual recovery decisions.

changes.rejected_passage: Keep the bundled engine version and source identity with CI output. The Rust dependency version alone is not what appears in a database error report. This fixture prints SQLite's runtime version and source ID and pins the C-library package in its Cargo manifest.
changes.replacement: This program uses rusqlite 0.41.0 with the bundled libsqlite3-sys 0.39.1 package. It prints SQLite’s runtime version and source ID as well. Keep those identifiers with a busy-error report, because the Rust wrapper’s version alone does not identify the engine that ran.
changes.reason: Name the pinned client/library versions and connect the evidence to an actual error report.

pending_limits: Temporary local WAL file, finite busy timeout and deliberate ordering; no exact-duration or throughput result.

articles.verdict: accepted only as progress while a submitted request is pending, with coordinator code fixes awaiting final CI; publication hold retained

changes.rejected_passage: title: "Keep rusqlite Calls off Tokio with a Bounded Database Worker"
changes.replacement: title: "Run rusqlite on a Worker Thread with a Bounded Tokio Queue"
changes.reason: The original title loosely implies Tokio cannot participate. Name the actual thread and channel arrangement.

changes.rejected_passage: summary: "Give a synchronous SQLite connection to one worker thread, bound its request queue, and check that another Tokio task can run while a write waits."
changes.replacement: summary: "Give one thread a SQLite connection, limit its request queue, and check that Tokio can run another task while a submitted write remains pending."
changes.reason: Keep the summary within what the readiness signal and heartbeat actually prove.

changes.rejected_passage: The worker signals that it reached the insert path before the test starts the heartbeat task. The separate connection still holds the writer lock. The test runs on a current-thread Tokio runtime, so the heartbeat demonstrates progress on the same async scheduler while database work remains elsewhere.
changes.replacement: The worker signals just before calling SQLite. The external connection still holds the writer lock, so the submitted insert cannot finish yet. On the current-thread Tokio runtime, the heartbeat checks that another async task can run while that request is pending. The signal does not mark the exact instant SQLite entered a lock wait.
changes.reason: Narrow observed-progress wording to the coordination actually present; avoid claiming a traced lock-wait entry.

changes.rejected_passage: This is a bounded progress check, not a latency benchmark. The one-second timeout is a failure bound for the controlled test. It does not establish an application's response-time target, and it is not a measured speedup over another database adapter.
changes.replacement: The one-second timeout makes a stalled heartbeat fail the test. It is not the service’s response-time target. In the application, set the queue wait and database wait from the same request budget so moving work to a thread does not merely move the long delay.
changes.reason: Remove repetitive non-benchmark wording and explain the practical limit on the fix.

changes.rejected_passage: Those assertions check that making other tasks responsive did not lose the database operation. They also show a clean stopping point: no more senders, no more queued jobs, and an owned worker thread that can exit.
changes.replacement: Both count replies must return one, after the insert replies successfully. That checks the order seen by queued jobs: they run after the saved note, rather than racing a different connection. Once the sender is dropped and the queue drains, the worker can exit.
changes.reason: Replace abstract success claims with the exact queue ordering and count expectations.

pending_limits: Readiness precedes execute; proves scheduler progress while request pending, not exact driver wait-start timing. Coordinator reports fixture println narrowed and thread join moved into spawn_blocking; final remote CI must include those changes. Queue slots do not bound arbitrary payload bytes or cancel started work.

articles.verdict: accepted after correcting ignored-PRAGMA wording and adding child-index guidance; publication hold retained

changes.rejected_passage: The returned connection has passed the setting check. A caller cannot forget a separate setup call after opening it. In a larger application, keep the raw connection opener private where practical and return an application store built from this initialized connection.
changes.replacement: A caller using this helper receives a connection with enforcement checked already. Keep the raw opener private where practical, so another request path cannot skip the helper by accident. Returning an application store instead of a raw connection can keep that setup in one place.
changes.reason: Avoid implying the helper makes every caller or external opener unable to bypass initialization.

changes.rejected_passage: The fixture closes the checked connection, opens another through the wrapper, and tries another orphan insert. That later connection must reject it too. It also attempts to enable enforcement inside a transaction on the deliberately unchecked connection and verifies that the setting stays off until the transaction ends.
changes.replacement: The fixture closes the checked connection, opens another through the wrapper, and tries another orphan insert. That later connection must reject it too. Separately, it tries to enable enforcement inside a transaction on the unchecked connection. The request has no effect: enforcement stays off. Ending that transaction does not apply the ignored request; enable it again outside the transaction when it is needed.
changes.reason: Correct the implication that the ignored PRAGMA may take effect automatically at transaction end.

changes.rejected_passage: Those checks are bounded and use a few temporary rows. They establish the application's initialization and deletion contract. They do not measure cascade performance on a large hierarchy or prove that an external program opening the same file uses the wrapper.
changes.replacement: For larger tables, inspect the child-side index too. The foreign key does not automatically create an index on members.project_id or tasks.project_id. Finding children during a parent deletion can otherwise require scanning the child table. The SQLite documentation linked above explains why those indexes are usually useful. Decide on them with representative data; this few-row example does not measure their cost.
changes.reason: Replace generic scope padding with a concrete performance trap documented in the same primary reference, without claiming a measured result.

changes.rejected_passage: When a join unexpectedly loses a row, inspect both sides of that boundary: what the Rust code passed, and what the writing connection enforced. Keeping the opener, the schema, and the negative insert test close together makes the next missing relationship easier to explain.
changes.replacement: If only imported tasks disappear from the join, inspect the import connection before changing the query. Check its foreign_keys setting, run foreign_key_check to find existing orphans, and choose a repair for those records. Fixing the opener prevents new damage; it does not recover the missing project or decide what an old task should belong to.
changes.reason: Replace a generic close with a specific diagnostic and repair sequence for the opening failure.

pending_limits: Existing orphan repair remains a business choice. Child indexes are advice for larger data, not part of the tiny fixture or a measured improvement. Test currently checks failed restricted deletion and final cascade; it does not explicitly assert both intermediate table counts after the restricted delete.
